questions.question: What are the 8 primitive data types in Java and what are their sizes?
questions.title: 8 Primitive Data Types in Java with Sizes
questions.direct_answer: Java has **8 primitive types**: `byte` (1 byte), `short` (2 bytes), `int` (4 bytes), `long` (8 bytes), `float` (4 bytes), `double` (8 bytes), `char` (2 bytes), and `boolean` (typically 1 bit). They are **not objects** — they live on the stack, hold values directly, and can't be `null`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Java knowledge and whether the candidate has actually used Java or just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing float/double sizes or forgetting that char is 2 bytes in Java (not 1 like C)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention default values (int → 0, boolean → false, char → \u0000) and that primitives can't be null

sections.title: Primitive Types: Java's Building Blocks
sections.content:
Java's **8 primitive types** are built directly into the language. Unlike objects, primitives store actual values rather than references, making them faster and more memory-efficient.

The **integer types** (`byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`) hold whole numbers of different ranges. The **floating-point types** (`float`, `double`) represent decimals. **`char`** stores a single Unicode character (16 bits). **`boolean`** holds only `true` or `false`. When you write `int count = 42;`, the value is stored directly in memory, not as an object — which is why primitives can't be `null` and are faster than wrappers (`Integer`, `Double`).

sections.title: The 8 Primitives at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Integer types|~Whole numbers|byte 1B, short 2B|int 4B (default)|long 8B (needs L)
blue|Floating-point|~Decimals|float 4B (needs f)|double 8B (default)|use BigDecimal for money
emerald|char + boolean|~char is 2B Unicode|single character|boolean true/false|not 1 byte like C
rose|Key traits|~Not objects|live on the stack|can't be null|defaults 0/false/\u0000

sections.title: Wrong — missing literal suffixes
sections.content:
```java
long big = 9999999999;  // COMPILE ERROR: int literal overflows
float price = 3.14;      // COMPILE ERROR: 3.14 is a double by default
```

sections.title: Right — L and f suffixes (and char is Unicode)
sections.content:
```java
long big = 9999999999L; // L suffix makes it a long literal
float price = 3.14f;     // f suffix makes it a float literal
char grade = 'A';        // 2 bytes (Unicode), not 1 like in C
// int x = null;         // would not compile — primitives can't be null
```

sections.title: Primitive Types in Action
When to Use Each Primitive Type
sections.content:
Use **`byte`** for small counters or flags when memory is tight.

Use **`int`** as the default integer — loop counters, array indices, most arithmetic.

Use **`long`** for timestamps (millis since epoch), file sizes, and large IDs.

Use **`double`** as the default for decimal math (use `BigDecimal` for currency).

Use **`char`** for single characters, **`boolean`** for flags. Prefer `double` over `float` unless memory-constrained.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting literal suffixes**: `long big = 9999999999;` fails (int overflow) — use `9999999999L`. `float x = 3.14;` fails — use `3.14f`.
- **Confusing char size**: Java `char` is 2 bytes (UTF-16), not 1 like C/C++.
- **Assuming primitives can be null**: `int count = null;` is a compile error — only reference types can be `null`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **8 primitives** — `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`.
- **Not objects** — stored directly on the stack; faster and leaner.
- **Cannot be null** — primitives always hold a value.
- **Defaults** — instance/static get `0`/`false`/`\u0000`; locals don't.
- **Sizes** — `int` 4B, `long` 8B, `char` 2B; `boolean` is JVM-dependent.
- **Suffixes** — `long` needs `L`, `float` needs `f`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Java has eight primitive data types that store values directly rather than references. The integer types are byte which is 1 byte, short which is 2 bytes, int which is 4 bytes, and long which is 8 bytes. For decimal numbers we have float at 4 bytes and double at 8 bytes. Then there's char for single Unicode characters at 2 bytes, and boolean for true or false values. The key thing to understand is that primitives aren't objects, they live on the stack and hold actual values. That's why they can't be null. For example, when you declare int count equals 10, the value 10 is stored directly in that memory location. This makes primitives much faster than their wrapper classes like Integer or Double. One gotcha is that char in Java is 2 bytes, not 1 byte like in C, because Java uses Unicode to support international characters. Also, when you're working with long or float values, you need to add the L or f suffix to your literals, otherwise the compiler treats them as int or double by default. In real code, you'd use int for most counting and loop indices, double for decimal math, and boolean for flags. Instance variables of primitive types get default values like zero or false, but local variables don't, you have to initialize them explicitly or the compiler will complain.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance variables, local variables, and static variables in Java?
questions.title: Instance vs Local vs Static Variables in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Instance variables** belong to an object (heap), get default values, and each object has its own copy. **Local variables** live inside a method (stack), have **no defaults**, and must be initialized before use. **Static variables** belong to the class (method area) and are shared across all instances.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java memory model and variable scoping rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking local variables get default values — they don't; the compiler errors on an uninitialized local variable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention where each lives (stack vs heap vs method area) and the thread-safety implications of static variables

sections.title: Three Flavors of Variables in Java
sections.content:
Java has three variable types with different lifetimes, scopes, and memory locations. **Instance variables** (fields) belong to an object — each new object gets its own copy. They live on the **heap** and exist as long as the object does. **Local variables** are declared inside methods or blocks — they live on the **stack** and vanish when the method returns. **Static variables** belong to the class itself — one copy shared by all instances, stored in the **method area**.

The critical distinction: instance and static variables get default values automatically (`0`, `false`, `null`), but local variables don't — you must initialize them before use or the compiler rejects your code.

sections.title: Instance vs Local vs Static at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Instance|~Per object|on the heap|default-initialized|one copy per object
blue|Local|~Inside a method|on the stack|NO default value|must initialize first
emerald|Static|~Per class|method area|shared by all instances|lives the whole program
rose|Watch out|~Statics + threads|need synchronization|locals are thread-safe|no instance access in static methods

sections.title: Instance vs Local vs Static Variables
sections.content:
| Aspect | Instance variable | Local variable | Static variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | Belongs to an object | Inside a method/block | Belongs to the class |
| Memory | Heap (with the object) | Stack (method frame) | Method area (shared) |
| Default value | Auto (0/false/null) | None — must initialize | Auto (0/false/null) |
| Lifetime | As long as the object | Until the method returns | Entire program runtime |
| Access | Via object reference | Only in declaring scope | Via class name or instance |

sections.title: Wrong — local variable has no default value
Right — locals initialized; instance/static auto-default
When to Use Each Variable Type
sections.content:
Use **instance variables** for state that varies between objects — a `User`'s name, email, age.

Use **local variables** for temporary work inside a method — loop counters, intermediate results. They're short-lived.

Use **static variables** for data shared across instances — a connection pool, app config, a counter of objects created, or `static final` constants. If two objects should share a value, make it static; if each needs its own, make it an instance variable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting local defaults**: `int count; System.out.println(count);` won't compile — locals must be initialized.
- **Accessing instance variables from static methods**: not allowed — static methods belong to the class, not an object.
- **Thread safety with statics**: static variables are shared across threads; modifying them without synchronization causes race conditions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Instance** — per object, on the heap, default-initialized.
- **Local** — inside a method, on the stack, no defaults, must initialize.
- **Static** — per class, method area, shared across instances and threads.
- **Memory model** — heap vs stack vs method area.
- **Initialization** — only locals cause a compile error if used uninitialized.
- **Thread safety** — statics need synchronization; locals are stack-isolated.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Java has three types of variables that differ in scope, lifetime, and memory location. Instance variables belong to an object. When you create a new Customer, that object gets its own copy of every instance variable like name or email. These live on the heap and last as long as the object exists. They automatically get default values, zero for numbers, false for booleans, null for references. Local variables are declared inside a method. They live on the stack and only exist while that method is running. Once the method returns, those variables disappear. The key difference here is that local variables don't get default values. If you declare int count and try to use it without assigning a value first, the compiler will stop you with an error. Static variables belong to the class itself, not to any particular instance. There's only one copy of a static variable shared by all objects of that class. They're stored in the method area and they last for the entire program runtime. Like instance variables, they do get default values. A common mistake is trying to access instance variables from a static method, that doesn't work because static methods don't have access to any particular object. Also, freshers often forget that static variables are shared across all threads, so if you're modifying them in a multi-threaded app, you need to handle synchronization to avoid race conditions.

questions.question: What will this code print — and why? `int a = 5; int b = a; b = 10; System.out.println(a);`
questions.title: Java Primitive Copy vs Reference Gotcha
questions.direct_answer: It prints **`5`**. Primitives in Java are **copied by value** — `int b = a` gives `b` its own copy of `5`. Changing `b` to `10` has no effect on `a`; they are completely independent variables.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands pass-by-value and the difference between primitives and objects in Java
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing this with object references where two variables can point to the same object
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with object reference behavior — if a and b both referenced the same object, mutating via b would affect what a sees

sections.title: Primitives Are Copied by Value
sections.content:
In Java, **primitive types** are always copied by value. Assigning one primitive to another, like `int b = a;`, copies the actual value from `a` into `b`. They become two independent variables, each with its own copy. Changing `b` has zero effect on `a`.

Like photocopying a document: writing on the copy leaves the original unchanged. This differs from **object references**, where assignment makes two variables point to the same object. With primitives you work with the actual value, not a reference. The **stack** gives each primitive its own memory, so there's no shared state — which is why local primitives are inherently thread-safe.

sections.title: Value Copy vs Reference Share at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Primitives|~Copied by value|int b = a copies 5|fully independent|changing b leaves a at 5
blue|Objects|~Copied by reference|both point to one object|shared state|mutating via one shows in the other
emerald|Method calls|~Also pass-by-value|primitive copied in|change inside is local|return to send a value back
rose|Why it matters|~No aliasing for primitives|stack-isolated|thread-safe locals|predictable debugging

sections.title: Primitives — independent copies
sections.content:
```java
int a = 5;
int b = a;   // b gets a COPY of 5
b = 10;      // changing b does not touch a
System.out.println(a); // 5
```

sections.title: Objects — shared reference
sections.content:
```java
var listA = new java.util.ArrayList<String>();
listA.add("Alice");
var listB = listA;   // listB points to the SAME object as listA
listB.add("Bob");    // mutation visible through listA too
System.out.println(listA.size()); // 2
```
Primitives copy the value; object variables copy the reference — that's the whole difference.

sections.title: Value Copying Even Through Method Calls
Why This Matters in Real Code
sections.content: Value copying matters when **passing primitives to methods** — the method gets a copy, so it can't change the caller's variable; you must `return` a modified value. It matters in **loops** when copying a counter, and in **debugging** — two primitives with different values are guaranteed independent, unlike object references that may share state. For **thread safety**, local primitives are inherently safe because each thread has its own stack frame.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting a link**: `int b = a;` doesn't connect the variables — they're separate.
- **Confusing with objects**: `List<String> listB = listA;` makes both point to the same list, so changes via one are visible through the other.
- **Thinking parameters are references**: passing an `int` and changing it inside doesn't affect the original — use a `return`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Value copying** — primitive assignment copies the value; variables are independent.
- **No shared state** — changing `b` after `int b = a` doesn't touch `a`.
- **Method parameters** — primitives are copied in; changes stay local.
- **Contrast with objects** — references share the same object.
- **Stack allocation** — each primitive gets its own stack slot.
- **Thread safety** — local primitives are inherently thread-safe.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: This code prints 5 because primitives in Java are copied by value. When you write int b equals a, Java copies the value 5 from a into b. At that point, a and b are two completely independent variables. They just happen to hold the same value. When you then change b to 10, you're only modifying b's memory location. The variable a is unaffected because it has its own separate copy of the value. It's like making a photocopy of a document, if you write on the copy, the original stays the same. This is really different from how objects work. If a and b were both List references pointing to the same ArrayList, then modifying the list through b would affect what you see through a, because they're both looking at the same object in memory. But with primitives, you're always working with the actual value, not a reference to something stored elsewhere. This behavior also affects method calls. If you pass an int to a method and the method changes that parameter, the original variable in the calling code is unaffected because the method received a copy. That's why if you want a method to return a modified int value, you have to use a return statement, you can't modify the original. Understanding this distinction between primitives and objects is fundamental to reasoning about Java code, especially when you're debugging or working with method parameters.

questions.question: What are valid variable naming conventions in Java, and what names are not allowed?
questions.title: Java Variable Naming Conventions and Rules
questions.direct_answer: Java variable names must **start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign** — never a digit. They are **case-sensitive**, can't be reserved keywords, and by convention use **camelCase** for variables/methods and **ALL_CAPS** for constants.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to Java conventions and basic language rules — separates those who've written Java from those who've just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the dollar sign is technically valid (though unusual), or assuming Java naming is the same as SQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the distinction between naming rules (compiler-enforced) and naming conventions (developer practice for readability)

sections.title: Java Variable Naming: Rules vs Conventions
sections.content:
Java naming has two layers: **compiler-enforced rules** and **community conventions**. The **rules** are strict: names must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign — not a digit. After the first character you can use letters, digits, underscores, or dollar signs. Names are **case-sensitive** (`count` and `Count` differ), and you can't use **reserved keywords** (`int`, `class`, `return`).

The **conventions** are softer but universal: **camelCase** for variables/methods (`firstName`), **PascalCase** for classes (`CustomerService`), and **ALL_CAPS with underscores** for constants (`MAX_RETRIES`). Good names are descriptive — `customerCount` over `c`.

sections.title: Naming Rules and Conventions at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Rules (compiler)|~Start letter/_/$|never a digit|case-sensitive|no reserved keywords
blue|Variables/methods|~camelCase|firstName|calculateTotal|first word lowercase
emerald|Classes/constants|~PascalCase classes|CustomerService|ALL_CAPS constants|MAX_RETRIES
rose|Good names|~Descriptive|customerCount over c|is/has/can for booleans|avoid cryptic abbreviations

sections.title: Wrong — names that won't compile
sections.content:
```java
int 1stPlace;     // COMPILE ERROR: starts with a digit
int my-variable;  // COMPILE ERROR: hyphen not allowed
int class;        // COMPILE ERROR: reserved keyword
```

sections.title: Right — valid names following conventions
sections.content:
```java
int firstPlace;                   // valid camelCase
String customerName = "Alice";     // descriptive
static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;  // constant: ALL_CAPS
```

sections.title: Case Sensitivity and Naming Styles
Choosing Good Variable Names
sections.content: Use **descriptive names** that reveal intent: `customerList` over `list`. For **loop counters**, single letters (`i`, `j`) are fine. For **booleans**, use `is`/`has`/`can` prefixes (`isActive`, `hasPermission`). For **collections**, use plurals (`orders`). For **constants**, ALL_CAPS with underscores (`MAX_SIZE`). Avoid cryptic abbreviations — `id` and `url` are fine, `custCnt` isn't.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Starting with a digit**: `int 1stPlace;` fails — use `firstPlace` or `place1`.
- **Using reserved keywords**: naming a variable `class` or `int` is a compile error.
- **Inconsistent casing**: mixing `customer_count` (snake_case) with Java's camelCase looks unprofessional.
- **Overly short names**: single letters for non-trivial variables hurt readability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **First char** — letter, underscore, or dollar sign; never a digit.
- **Subsequent chars** — letters, digits, underscores, dollar signs.
- **Case-sensitive** — `count` and `Count` are different.
- **No keywords** — `int`, `class`, `return` are reserved.
- **camelCase** — variables/methods; **PascalCase** — classes.
- **ALL_CAPS** — constants (`static final`).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Java variable naming has strict rules enforced by the compiler and softer conventions followed by the community. The compiler rules are that a variable name must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign. It can't start with a digit. After the first character, you can use letters, digits, underscores, or dollar signs in any combination. Names are case-sensitive, so count and Count are two different variables. You also can't use reserved keywords like int, class, or public as variable names, the compiler will reject those. Dollar sign is technically allowed, but you almost never see it in real code except in generated classes. Beyond the compiler rules, there are strong conventions. Variables and methods use camelCase, the first word is lowercase and subsequent words are capitalized, like firstName or calculateTotal. Class names use PascalCase where even the first letter is capitalized, like CustomerService. Constants use ALL CAPS with underscores, like MAX CONNECTIONS or DEFAULT TIMEOUT. These conventions aren't enforced by the compiler, but every professional codebase follows them because they make code instantly readable. A common mistake freshers make is trying to start a variable name with a digit, like 1stPlace, which won't compile. You'd need to write firstPlace or place1 instead. Another mistake is using reserved keywords. Also, be aware that Java naming is different from languages like Python that use snake case with underscores. In Java, we use camelCase, so it's userCount not user underscore count. The key is that good names are descriptive.

questions.question: What is the var keyword in Java and when should you use it?
questions.title: var Keyword and Local Type Inference in Java 10
questions.direct_answer: The **`var`** keyword (Java 10) is **local type inference** — the compiler infers the variable's type from the initializer. It works **only for local variables with an initializer**, never for fields, parameters, return types, or a `null` initializer. Java stays statically typed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern Java features and understanding that var doesn't make Java dynamically typed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking var means dynamic typing like JavaScript — Java is still statically typed; the type is fixed at compile time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that var reduces boilerplate with generics, and explain where it cannot be used (fields, parameters, null initializer)

sections.title: Local Variable Type Inference with var
sections.content:
**`var`** (Java 10) reduces boilerplate by letting the compiler infer a local variable's type from its initializer. `var orders = new ArrayList<Order>();` infers `ArrayList<Order>` from the right-hand side.

This is **static type inference** — the type is fixed at compile time; Java stays statically typed. It's especially handy with verbose generics like `Map<String, List<Customer>>`. The constraint: `var` works only for **local variables with initializers** — not fields, parameters, return types, or `null` initializers (the compiler can't infer a type from `null`). Use it when the type is obvious from context, not when it makes code cryptic.

sections.title: var at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|var|~Local type inference|Java 10+|compiler reads the right side|still statically typed
blue|Allowed|~Locals with initializer|var x = 42;|for (var o : list)|great with generics
emerald|Not allowed|~No fields/params/returns|no null initializer|no declaration without init|type locked at compile time
rose|Use it|~When type is obvious|cuts boilerplate|readability over brevity|don't make readers guess

sections.title: Wrong — var without a usable initializer
sections.content:
```java
var user = null;  // COMPILE ERROR: can't infer a type from null
var temp;         // COMPILE ERROR: var needs an initializer
```

sections.title: Right — var with a clear initializer
sections.content:
```java
var message = "hello";                               // inferred String
var count = 0;                                       // inferred int
var map = new java.util.HashMap<String, Integer>();  // cuts generic boilerplate
// count = "text";  // still statically typed — this would NOT compile
```

sections.title: Where var Works and Where It Doesn't
When to Use var
sections.content: Use **`var`** when the type is obvious from the right-hand side — `var service = new OrderService();`. It shines with verbose generics and in loops: `for (var order : orders)`. **Avoid** it when the initializer is a method call whose return type isn't obvious — `var result = service.process(data);` makes readers guess. The guideline: if someone must hover in an IDE to know the type, spell it out.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking var is dynamic typing**: once `var count = 5;` infers `int`, you can't assign a `String` later — the type is locked.
- **Using var with null**: `var user = null;` fails — no type to infer.
- **Overusing var**: `var x = calculate();` with a non-obvious return type hurts readability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Local type inference** — compiler infers the type from the initializer.
- **Still static** — the type is fixed at compile time.
- **Locals only** — not fields, parameters, or return types.
- **Needs an initializer** — and it can't be `null`.
- **Great with generics** — cuts verbose declarations.
- **Readability over brevity** — use it when the type is obvious.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The var keyword was added in Java 10 for local variable type inference. It lets you skip writing the full type name when the compiler can figure it out from the right-hand side. For example, instead of writing ArrayList less than Order greater than orders equals new ArrayList less than Order greater than, you can write var orders equals new ArrayList less than Order greater than. The compiler infers the type from the initializer. It's important to understand that this is still static typing. Once the compiler decides orders is an ArrayList of Order, that type is locked in at compile time. You can't later reassign orders to a String. Java doesn't become dynamically typed just because you use var. The restrictions are that var only works for local variables inside methods. You can't use it for class fields, method parameters, or return types. Also, you must initialize the variable right away, you can't declare var x and then assign it later, because the compiler needs the initializer to figure out the type. And you can't initialize var to null because the compiler has no way to infer a specific type from null. The main benefit is reducing boilerplate, especially with complex generic types. But you should only use var when the type is obvious. The rule is readability over brevity, if someone has to hover in their IDE to figure out what type result is, just spell out the type explicitly.

questions.question: What does the final keyword do when applied to a variable in Java?
questions.title: final Variables in Java — Constants and Immutable References
questions.direct_answer: **`final`** on a variable means it can be **assigned only once**. For primitives the value can't change; for object references the **reference** can't be repointed — but the object's internal state can still be mutated. It's the reference that's final, not the object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the distinction between a final reference and an immutable object — a classic gotcha
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking final makes an object immutable — it only prevents reassignment of the reference, not modification of the object's contents
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify the difference between a final reference and a truly immutable object, and mention final instance variables must be initialized in the constructor or at declaration

sections.title: What final Really Means
sections.content:
**`final`** on a variable creates a constant binding — assign it once, then you can't reassign. For **primitives** this is simple: `final int max = 100;` means `max` is always `100`. For **object references** it's subtler. `final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` makes the *reference* `names` final, not the list — you can't repoint `names`, but you can still add, remove, or clear elements.

Like a house address in permanent marker: the address can't change, but you can renovate the house. **`final` prevents reassignment, not mutation.** True immutability requires designing the class so its state can't change (like `String`).

sections.title: final at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|final variable|~Assign exactly once|reassignment = compile error|documents intent|catches bugs early
blue|On primitives|~Value is locked|final int MAX = 100|a true constant|can't change
emerald|On references|~Reference is locked|can't repoint|but the object CAN mutate|names.add() still works
rose|True immutability|~Needs more than final|no setters + final fields|List.of(), String|design the class

sections.title: Wrong — assuming a final reference is immutable
Right — for true immutability, lock the object too
final: Assignment vs Mutation
When to Use final
sections.content: Use **`final`** for true constants (`final double PI = 3.14159;`), for parameters to prevent accidental reassignment, and for instance variables set once during construction (an ID, a timestamp). Use it with collections when you want a stable reference but still modify contents. Many teams use `final` liberally because it makes code more predictable and catches reassignment bugs early.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing final reference with immutability**: `final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();` still allows `items.add(...)`. `final` only blocks reassigning `items`.
- **Not initializing final instance variables**: they must be set at declaration or in every constructor, or it's a compile error.
- **Thinking final freezes the object globally**: another method holding the same reference can still mutate the object.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single assignment** — `final` variables are assigned exactly once.
- **Primitives vs references** — value locked vs reference locked.
- **Mutation allowed** — a `final` reference's object can still change.
- **True immutability** — needs no setters and final fields (e.g., `String`).
- **Instance variables** — must be initialized at declaration or in the constructor.
- **Constants** — combine `static final` with ALL_CAPS naming.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The final keyword on a variable means you can only assign it once. After that initial assignment, you can't change it. For primitive types like int or double, this is straightforward, final int max equals 100 means max will always be 100. But for object references, it's more nuanced. When you declare final List less than String greater than names equals new ArrayList, you're making the reference final, not the list itself. You can't reassign names to point at a different list, but you can absolutely modify the list's contents. You can add items, remove items, clear it, all of that is allowed because you're not changing what names points to, you're just mutating the object it refers to. This is a common source of confusion. Final doesn't make an object immutable. It only prevents reassignment of the reference. If you want true immutability, you need to design your class so its state can't be changed after construction, like how String works, or use something like List dot of. For instance variables, final has an additional rule, you must initialize them either where you declare them or in the constructor. The compiler enforces this. In practice, final is really useful for documenting intent. When you mark something final, you're telling other developers that this value shouldn't change. It also helps prevent bugs because the compiler catches any accidental reassignment immediately. A lot of teams use final liberally for parameters and local variables because it makes code more predictable.
